q: A Spanish denomination may cover authorised parcels in Catalonia, Rioja, Navarra, Aragon and Extremadura at once. Which one?
exp: Cava was drawn around a method and a register of approved plots rather than one boundary, which is why it stretches across the country. The great majority of it still comes from Penedes.

q: Which three varieties make up the traditional white Cava blend?
exp: Macabeo brings fruit and is the same grape as Rioja's Viura, Xarel-lo brings body and structure, and Parellada brings acidity from higher, cooler sites. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are permitted additions.

q: How long must a Cava labelled Gran Reserva rest on its lees?
exp: Thirty months at minimum, against a floor of nine for the basic category. Lees contact is what builds the toast and bread-dough character that separates a serious Cava from a cheap one.

q: The first Spanish sparkling wine of the traditional method was bottled in 1872 by a member of which house?
exp: Josep Raventos came back from Champagne and bottled the first, using local varieties rather than imported ones. Freixenet, also of Sant Sadurni, became the trade's other giant.

q: For most of its first century this wine was sold under a borrowed French word. What forced the change to the name Cava?
opts: A shortage of the traditional grapes
European rules reserving Champagne to its own region
A Spanish tax on foreign trade names
A change in the method of production
exp: The trade dropped champana and took cava, the word for the underground cellar where the bottles rest. Nothing about the wine itself changed with the name.

q: Granite posts hold vines on overhead frames well clear of the ground in Rias Baixas. Which problem is that solving?
opts: Frost settling on the lower slopes
Fungal disease in a very wet climate
Excessive summer heat on the fruit
exp: The parral lifts the canopy clear of the damp air near the ground, so that air moves through it and the fruit dries after rain, on a coast that can take well over a metre of it a year. It also let a smallholder grow vegetables underneath.

q: Which Rias Baixas subzone is the coolest, the nearest to the sea and the historic heart of Albarino?
exp: Salnes sits around Cambados on the Ria de Arousa and gives the most bracing, saline wines. Condado do Tea lies inland up the Mino and is the warmest of the subzones.

q: Rescued from near-extinction in the 1970s, one white variety now defines Valdeorras. Which is it?
exp: Godello is broader and stonier than Albarino and takes well to lees ageing and a little oak. Valdeorras lies inland on slate at the eastern edge of Galicia.

q: Terraces cut into gorges above the Sil and the Mino are worked by hand and sometimes reached by boat. Which denomination?
exp: The slopes reach gradients no machine can work, which is why the region is a byword for heroic viticulture. Mencia is its principal red grape.

q: On the Basque coast a sharp, low-alcohol white with a faint prickle is drunk young as an aperitif. What is it called?
exp: Txakoli comes from three small Basque denominations and is built mainly on Hondarrabi Zuri. It is bottled with a trace of carbon dioxide and drunk within the year.

q: A Rioja house went looking for a white grape in the 1970s and replanted an old Castilian variety. Which denomination grew out of that?
exp: Marques de Riscal wanted a white to sit beside its Rioja reds and settled on Verdejo. Rueda was recognised in 1980, the first denomination in Castilla y Leon.

q: Before Verdejo was replanted, Rueda's reputation rested on a very different wine. What was it?
opts: An oxidatively aged white called dorado
exp: Dorado was aged in glass demijohns and part-filled barrels under a film of yeast, closer to a light Sherry than to any modern white. A little of it is still made.

q: Dry Garnacha rosado made the name of a denomination that shares part of its ground with Rioja. Which one?
exp: Part of Rioja Oriental lies inside Navarra, and the two have shared grapes and history for centuries. Navarra also plants more Cabernet, Merlot and Chardonnay than most Spanish denominations.

q: Steep slate slopes in a sheltered basin in the province of Leon give fragrant, lightly built reds. Which denomination?
exp: El Bierzo sits in a bowl between the Galician mountains and the Castilian plateau, taking Atlantic rain with continental heat. Old ungrafted Mencia on slate is its calling card.

q: Spain's most widely planted white variety covers the hot central plateau and goes in quantity to the brandy stills. Which grape?
exp: Airen survives drought on poor soil, planted wide apart as low bushes across La Mancha. Its wine is neutral, which is what a still wants, and the Tempranillo beside it goes by Cencibel.

q: A guest assumes an Oloroso must be sweet because it is dark. What do you tell them?
opts: It is dry, unless it has been sweetened for a cream blend
Its sweetness comes from the flor
It is always sweet, being made from raisined grapes
exp: Every dry Sherry, all of them from Palomino, ferments out. The colour and the walnut smell come from years of oxygen, and sweetness in a dark Sherry has been blended in afterwards. The naturally sweet Pedro Ximenez and Moscatel are the exceptions, pressed from sun-dried grapes and fortified before the sugar is gone.
